title: Centre Airlifts 250 RAF Personnel to Arunachal After Violent Siang Dam Protests
excerpt: Two RAF companies were flown from Navi Mumbai to Pasighat after an NHPC office and a police station were torched during protests against the 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project.
body:
• The Centre has airlifted two Rapid Action Force companies, about 250 CRPF personnel, from Navi Mumbai to Pasighat after violence over the proposed 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project.
  • A mob torched an NHPC office and a police station on Friday night and vandalised the homes of three political leaders, including the state BJP chief, according to police; Mirror Now reported more than 40 police personnel injured.
  • Chief Minister Pema Khandu said peaceful protest is a democratic right but must stay within the law, and called the Pasighat incidents regrettable.
  • Opposition centres on the Adi community's fears of displacement and loss of ancestral land, while the government presents the project partly as a strategic counter to China's upstream dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo.

The Centre has dispatched two companies of the Rapid Action Force (RAF) to Arunachal Pradesh after protests against the proposed 11,200-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project turned violent in Pasighat, officials said on Sunday. The Ministry of Home Affairs directed on Saturday that the RAF companies, comprising about 250 personnel, be airlifted from Navi Mumbai aboard an Indian Air Force transport aircraft, according to The Hindu BusinessLine's PTI report. The units were expected to reach Pasighat and deploy by Sunday.

The RAF is the CRPF's specialist anti-riot unit, identifiable by its blue uniforms. Multiple CRPF units were already in the violence-affected areas, officials said, and Arunachal Pradesh has a permanent deployment of about two to three CRPF battalions. Officials said CRPF personnel had handled the protests since Friday and prevented the violence from escalating further, though several police and central forces personnel were injured.

What Happened in Pasighat

A 12-hour bandh across Siang, Upper Siang and East Siang districts on Friday remained largely peaceful, according to a statement from the Chief Minister's Office. Violence erupted in Pasighat after the bandh ended and continued until about 3.30 a.m. on Saturday. A mob torched an NHPC office and a police station and vandalised the residences of three political leaders, including that of the state BJP chief, in East Siang district, Arunachal Pradesh Police officials said.

Mirror Now reported more than 40 police personnel injured in stone-pelting and one protester hospitalised after being struck by a tear gas shell. The East Siang district administration has imposed prohibitions on public gatherings and processions across Pasighat, Mebo and Ruksin, the report said.

"The right to peaceful protest was an essential part of democracy, but it was important that demonstrations remained within the bounds of the law and did not result in damage to property or disruption of public order."

— Pema Khandu, Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh

Why the Siang Project Is Contested

The Siang is the main stem of the Brahmaputra in Arunachal Pradesh: it is the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet and becomes the Brahmaputra in Assam. The proposed multipurpose project would store and regulate that flow, generate 11,200 MW, and — in the government's framing — act as a buffer against China's planned mega dam upstream on the Yarlung Tsangpo.

For the indigenous Adi community, the stakes are local and immediate. Residents fear displacement, loss of livelihoods and ancestral land, and damage to a river tied to their cultural identity. Opposition has intensified in recent weeks as security personnel moved in to facilitate surveys and drilling for the project's pre-feasibility report, and after four protesters were detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014. The Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum has urged a boycott of government consultations, and Union Minister Kiren Rijiju has previously called for dialogue with senior Adi community members.

Two Arguments That Have Not Met

The government maintains that the current work is a pre-feasibility assessment, not final construction approval, and that the project would improve water and energy security and create jobs. Protest groups argue that survey work under heavy security is itself a step toward land acquisition, and that affected families must be heard before the process moves forward. Those positions explain why a technical survey has become a law-and-order crisis: one side sees a strategic national project at its earliest study stage, the other sees an irreversible decision being prepared without consent.

What Happens Next

The immediate test is whether the RAF deployment holds the peace in Pasighat without further injuries while prohibitory orders remain in force. The longer test is political: whether the state government opens a structured dialogue with Adi organisations and protest groups before further survey work, and whether detentions and the consultation boycott harden or ease. For readers outside the Northeast, the outcome matters beyond one district — it will shape how India builds strategic infrastructure on transboundary rivers where national security, tribal rights and ecology collide.
